prs.title: turbo-tasks: count task executions in task statistics
prs.author: sokra
prs.body:
### What?

Adds an `executions` counter to turbo-tasks task statistics (`NEXT_TURBOPACK_TASK_STATISTICS`). It counts how often a task of each function started executing.

```json
"next_core::next_config::NextConfig::from_string": { "cache_hit": 1, "cache_miss": 0, "executions": 1 }
```

- **What's counted:** `cache_hit` / `cache_miss` count function calls that found or created a task, as before. `executions` counts actual executions, including re-executions of existing tasks after an invalidation.
- **Where:** the counter is recorded in `try_start_task_execution` once a cached task has been taken from `Scheduled` and is about to run. Transient root tasks have no function and aren't counted.
- **Cost:** there's no overhead beyond the existing `Option` check when statistics are disabled.
- **Test:** a new test in `turbo-tasks-backend/tests/task_statistics.rs` covers fresh executions, cache hits without execution, and a re-execution after an invalidation whose lookup still counts as a hit.

### Why?

`cache_miss` only counts a task *type* that isn't in memory or the persistent cache. A restored task that is dirty re-executes, but its callers record a `cache_hit`, so the statistics can't show which work a warm build actually redid.

Example: in #100780, moving a project with its build cache re-runs `NextConfig::from_string` and 13 other functions, yet the statistics report **no** misses. With `executions`, the statistics show exactly the functions that a turbo-tasks trace shows. 
…(truncated)

prs.title: Keep dev overlay errors across no-op webpack hot updates
prs.author: sokra
prs.body:
### What?

Webpack dev no longer clears dev-overlay errors on a hot update that changes no modules.

This fixes the flaky `dev - client navigation` cases in `test/e2e/app-dir/instant-validation/suspense-boundaries{,.partial-prefetching}.test.ts` and `head-and-reporting{,.partial-prefetching}.test.ts`. They failed with `Redbox did not open.` in `test dev` (webpack) jobs.

### Why?

A soft navigation to a route that hasn't been compiled yet makes webpack compile it on demand. The browser then gets a `building`/`built` HMR cycle whose hot update has **no updated modules**. `tryApplyUpdatesWebpack` still ran a full Fast Refresh cycle for it (`onBeforeRefresh` → `apply` → `onRefresh`).

The overlay reducer's `ACTION_REFRESH` keeps only errors received *after* `onBeforeRefresh`. Instant validation sends its error to the browser for the same navigation. When that error arrived after `building` but before `module.hot.check()` resolved, the no-op refresh dropped it and the issues badge never appeared. Every failing CI log shows the browser logging the validation error a few ms before `[Fast Refresh] done`.

This affects any server-sent dev error that races with a no-op webpack update, not only these tests.

### How?

- Only dispatch `onBeforeRefresh` when the update has changed modules.
- Only dispatch the matching `onRefresh` when this update chain started one. A pending refresh carries over when an update is re-checked because a newer one arrived.
- `module.hot.apply()` still runs f

prs.title: turbo-tasks-backend: merge aggregated data updates for new followers
prs.author: sokra
prs.body:
### What?

Resolves the `TODO merge AggregatedDataUpdate` in `inner_of_upper_has_new_followers` (turbo-tasks-backend aggregation update queue). The diffs produced while connecting several new followers to an upper are now merged into a single `AggregatedDataUpdate`, and at most one `AggregatedDataUpdateJob` is enqueued for the upper's uppers.

### Why?

When an upper gains N new inner followers, applying their data produced up to N diffs, and each one was enqueued as its own job with a clone of the same `upper_ids`. Every one of those jobs then locks and updates each grand-upper separately, even though a single combined update has the same net effect.

### How?

- New `AggregatedDataUpdate::merge`:
  - Dirty container updates are summed per field. All diffs returned by `apply` on the same task carry that task's id, which is a documented precondition and checked with a debug assertion. If the sums cancel to zero, the dirty container update is dropped.
  - Collectible entries are concatenated. The existing `optimize` then sums them per collectible and drops zero entries, so `+1`/`-1` pairs from successive diffs cancel.
- At the call site, the diffs are merged and optimized after the upper's lock is released. The optimize pass is skipped when there is only a single diff. Nothing is enqueued if the merged update is empty or the upper has no uppers.
- Applying the merged update gives the same final counts and the same net presence changes as applying the diffs one after another. O
…(truncated)

prs.author: sokra
prs.body:
### What?

Adds an e2e test that checks whether the Turbopack filesystem build cache survives moving the project to another directory. It also fixes the first portability problems the test found.

It relies on the `executions` counter in turbo-tasks task statistics, added in #101025.

### Why?

A restored build cache should still be valid when the project sits at a different absolute path. That happens with CI checkouts, Docker build contexts, and caches restored into another workspace. - Each case runs a cold `next build`, a warm build in the same directory, then moves the whole project root (including `.next`) and runs another warm build.

prs.title: Turbopack: scale default disk write concurrency
prs.author: sokra
prs.body:
### What?

On Linux, Turbopack's default disk write concurrency now scales with available parallelism instead of using a fixed limit of 4. The Linux default is `clamp(available_parallelism, 4, 16)`, using `turbo_tasks::parallel::available_parallelism()` so CPU affinity and `TURBO_TASKS_AVAILABLE_PARALLELISM` are respected.

**macOS, Windows and all other platforms stay at the current fixed default of 4**, pending measurements on those platforms. Their limits (e.g. open file limits on macOS, metadata contention on NTFS) differ from Linux. `TURBO_ENGINE_WRITE_CONCURRENCY` still overrides the default on every platform.

### Why?

On larger machines, writing many small build outputs was throttled by the fixed limit. This is part of the build scaling work in #100250.

### How?

- The scaling default is gated with `cfg(target_os = "linux")`. Other platforms compile to the fixed default of 4.
- On Linux, 4 is the minimum and the fallback when parallelism can't be determined.
- On Linux, the cap of 16 limits open file handles and blocked tokio workers. A limit of 32 or 64 did not make builds faster in the sweep below.
- EMFILE retry handling is unchanged.

Moving writes to `spawn_blocking` is left out. The write path borrows content and path state and has retry and tracing behavior, so that change needs its own design and benchmark. In these runs, limits up to 64 did not show a measurable cold-build compile regression, despite IO currently blocking tokio workers.

prs.title: Turbopack: don't grow effect vectors inside the analyzer arena
prs.author: jimmyhmiller
prs.body:
The analyzer collects effects into bump-allocated vectors while it walks a module. A bump arena can't free memory, so every time one of those vectors grows, its old buffer stays allocated until the analysis finishes. Effect vectors grow constantly, so a large part of the arena ends up being abandoned buffers.

Collect effects in heap vectors instead, and copy each finished block into the arena at its exact size. The arena then only holds what is actually kept, as intended when effects moved into the arena in #94614.

No change in output. Measured on analyze_ecmascript_module alone, release build, 5 alternating rounds against the parent commit, as median paired changes:

| Input                 | Peak memory | Bytes allocated | Allocations | CPU   |
| --------------------- | ----------- | --------------- | ----------- | ----- |
| 8,000 modules         | -20.1%      | -8.4%           | +3.3%       | -0.9% |
| Generated stress      | -22.3%      | -14.9%          | +0.0%       | -1.0% |
| Four large benchmarks | +0.0%       | +6.7%           | +3.1%       | -4.1% |

Peak memory is the sum of each module's peak live allocations. On the 8,000 modules it goes from 7,652 MB to 6,118 MB. The CPU changes are within noise. The four large benchmark files gain bytes from the heap vectors' own growth and the final copy, without a change in peak.

prs.title: turbo-persistence: make batch_get callback-oriented
prs.author: lukesandberg
prs.body:
## What?

`TurboPersistence::batch_get` no longer returns an ordered `Vec<Option<ArcBytes>>`. It now reports each key to a callback:

```rust
pub fn batch_get<K: QueryKey + Sync>(
    &self,
    family: usize,
    keys: &[K],
    on_result: impl Fn(usize, Option<ArcBytes>) -> Result<()> + Sync,
) -> Result<()>
```

- `on_result` gets the index of the key in `keys`, and its value, or `None` when the key is missing or deleted.
- On success it has been called exactly once per index, including each occurrence of a duplicate key. The calls are in no particular order and may run concurrently on the scheduler's threads: for batches above the parallel threshold, the callbacks run inside the parallel chunks.
- A read error or a callback error is returned. Other callbacks may already have run, and some indices may never be reported.
- `on_result` runs while the database holds its internal read lock, so it must not call back into the database.

The turbo-tasks backend is updated the whole way down:

- `TurboKeyValueDatabase::batch_get`, `TurboBackingStorage::batch_lookup_data` and `restore_task_data_batch` take the same kind of callback.
- `batch_lookup_data` decodes `TaskStorage` inside the callback.
- The batched restore in `prepare_tasks_with_callback` stores each decoded result in its `TaskRestoreEntry` directly. The entry's result fields are now `OnceLock`s, so the writes stay safe.
- If a batch fails, every claimed entry still gets the batch error, replacing any result already sto
…(truncated)

prs.title: turbo-tasks: avoid redundant aggregation roots and root-upper optimization cascades
prs.author: sokra
prs.body:
## Summary

Two fixes in `turbo-tasks-backend` for cases where reading **already computed** tasks from a new root, or from a parentless `turbo_tasks::run` closure, restructures large parts of the aggregation graph. Context: #100250. The motivating pattern is a new root operation reading the existing endpoint outputs after the emit, like the route bundle stats in #101540.

### A: count all root uppers as one upper in `optimize_task`

`optimize_task` raises a task's aggregation number when `(uppers - 1) * followers` is too large. A root aggregates its whole subgraph, and raising the number never removes an upper edge to a root, yet root uppers were still counted.

So every additional root over an existing subgraph made large parts of it look like they needed optimization. The resulting raises cascaded into a rebalance of the subgraph without reducing upper edges. The old code already counted a `root_uppers` variable but never used it, and it also counted root *followers*.

The fix:
- Count only root **uppers**, persistent or transient.
- Treat them as a single upper when evaluating the threshold and seeding the search.

Behavior with at most one root upper is unchanged.

### B: parentless calls no longer make persistent callees aggregation roots

`connect_child` made every child connected without a parent task (e.g. called from a `turbo_tasks::run` closure) an aggregation root, so each one aggregated its entire, possibly large and existing, subgraph.

Making the callee a root i
…(truncated)

prs.title: turbo-tasks: don't make parentless transient tasks aggregation roots
prs.author: sokra
prs.body:
## Summary

Follow-up to #101604, from [this review comment](https://github.com/vercel/next.js/pull/101604#discussion_r4548045743).

#101604 stopped making parentless persistent callees, such as tasks called from a `turbo_tasks::run` closure, aggregation roots. This PR does the same for parentless **transient** callees.

The same argument applies to transient tasks:
- A parentless connect has no upper, so there is nothing to shield.
- Tasks that need to be roots already are:
  - Strongly consistent reads and collectibles reads are only allowed on `root` functions. The check is based on the task's function and applies to transient function tasks as well.
  - `root` functions are made roots when they are created, whether persistent or transient.
  - Top-level transient tasks (root and once tasks) are created with the maximum aggregation number.

Now `connect_child` only makes a task a root when a transient parent calls a persistent child. That rule shields the persistent graph from the transient caller and is unchanged.

The "already constructed root" shortcut is removed. It only applied to the parentless transient case, so it is dead code now.

## Verification

- `connect_child` unit test: a parentless transient child is not made a root. This test is flipped from the previous behavior.
- New integration test `parentless_calls_of_transient_tasks_are_only_roots_if_root_functions`:
  - A transient non-root function called from `run` is not a root, and is still held by a transient

prs.title: Turbopack: start whole-app client style groups earlier in production builds
prs.author: sokra
prs.body:
### What?

In production Turbopack builds, compute the whole-app client style groups as soon as their inputs are ready, rather than when the first client chunk group that contains CSS asks for them.

`output_assets_operation` now runs `compute_whole_app_client_style_groups_early` concurrently with the endpoint outputs. That function requests `ModuleGraph::style_groups` with the same full module graph, client chunking context and style chunking config that `make_style_production_chunks` uses later, so the chunker reuses the same task. It skips the work when:

- the build is not production or uses per-page module graphs;
- the whole-app graph has no reachable `StyleModule` (apps without CSS never compute style groups today).

Output does not change.

### Why?

In CSS-heavy, route-heavy App Router builds, the loose style-groups computation is one mostly sequential task over all chunk groups. It needs only the chunk group info and the module batches. Today it starts lazily, after the merged-modules computation and the first endpoint's per-layout SSR chunk groups. That puts several seconds of single-threaded work on the critical path, while the rest of the machine waits for chunking to begin.

Benchmark app: 5,000 generated routes plus section index pages, 500 route handlers, 3,000 components (from the generator in #101502). In a traced 32-CPU cold build:

- **Before:** `compute style groups loose` started 1.7 s after merged modules ended, ran 3.7 s at ~1 busy CPU, and blocked the
…(truncated)

prs.title: create-next-app: exit with code 1 when installation fails
prs.author: sokra
prs.body:
## Summary

When dependency installation fails, `create-next-app` prints `Aborting installation. <pm> install has failed.` but exits with code **0**. Scripts and CI calling `create-next-app` therefore see a false success.

`exit()` awaited `notifyUpdate()`, which unconditionally called `process.exit(0)`, so the following `process.exit(1)` was unreachable. `notifyUpdate()` no longer exits. The success path now exits with `0` explicitly after the update notice, and the failure path exits with `1`.

This surfaced in a canary CI failure of `test/production/create-next-app/templates/pages.test.ts`. A transient `npm ERR! code ETARGET` during install (an upstream package release published non-atomically) was reported as `missing expected file node_modules/next` instead of failing the `exitCode` assertion, because CNA exited 0.

## Verification

- New test `should exit with a non-zero code when dependency installation fails` in `test/production/create-next-app/index.test.ts`. It installs from a missing local tarball, so it needs no network.
  - Before the fix: fails (`Expected: 1, Received: 0`).
  - After the fix: passes 3/3.
- `NEXT_TEST_MODE=start IS_WEBPACK_TEST=1 node run-tests.js --retries 0 --runs 3 -c 1 test/production/create-next-app/index.test.ts`: 3/3 passed.
- `test/production/create-next-app/templates/pages.test.ts` (success path, exit 0) still passes with a warm npm cache.

prs.title: turbo-persistence: report batch_get misses from batch_lookup_entry
prs.author: sokra
prs.body:
Follow-up to #100678, from a review comment there.

## What?

`batch_get` now reports missing keys while it walks the SST files of a shard, instead of doing a separate pass over the keys afterwards.

- `MetaFile::batch_lookup_entry` takes an `is_last` flag and an `on_miss` callback, next to `on_found`.
- On the last (oldest) SST file of the shard, it walks every key that is still unresolved and reports the misses through `on_miss`:
  - keys outside the file's hash range, without a lookup;
  - keys inside the range that miss the quick filter or the SST lookup.
- On every other file nothing changes: only the keys in its hash range are visited, and nothing is reported as missing, since an older file may still hold the key.
- `batch_get_chunk` passes `is_last` from the file's position in the shard. Its `on_miss` reports `None` for the key and counts `not_found`. A shard without any SST files reports all its keys as missing.

## Why?

The pass after the SST loop walked all keys of the chunk once more to find the unresolved ones. The last file already walks the keys, so it can report the misses itself.

## How?

- The lookup stops early once all keys of a chunk are found, as before; there is nothing left to report then.
- The `batch_get` contract is unchanged: every index is reported exactly once (found, `None` for a tombstone or a missing key), and callback errors are returned.
- The statistics keep their meaning.
- A new test, `batch_get_misses_outside_last_sst_range`, covers:

prs.author: sokra
prs.body:
### What?

Fixes the `pnpm-lock.yaml` entry for `bench/large-app-router` so that `pnpm install --frozen-lockfile` works on canary again.

### Why?

Since #101502 was merged, canary CI (`build`, `build-next`, `fetch test timings`, `test devlow package`, …) fails at install with:

```
ERR_PNPM_LOCKFILE_MISSING_DEPENDENCY
Broken lockfile: no entry for 'lucide-react@0.554.0(react@19.3.0-canary-e84e1492-20261031)' in pnpm-lock.yaml
```

#101587 upgraded React to `19.3.0-canary-1620f7b9-20261111` while #101502 was open. The lockfile changes merged without a textual conflict. However, the new `bench/large-app-router` importer still referenced the `lucide-react` snapshot that was resolved against the old React version, and #101587 had removed that snapshot.

### How?

Point the importer at the existing `lucide-react@0.554.0(react@19.3.0-canary-1620f7b9-20261111)` snapshot. This is a one-line lockfile change.

### Verification

- On current canary with this change, `pnpm install --frozen-lockfile` succeeds.
- A plain `pnpm install` leaves the lockfile unchanged ("Already up to date").
- `pnpm-lock.yaml` has no remaining references to `e84e1492`.

prs.title: turbo-tasks-backend: read collectibles and update the reader dependency atomically
prs.author: sokra
prs.body:
### What?

Keep a task that reads collectibles from keeping stale collectibles when they change while it reads them. After `read_strongly_consistent()`, the reader now always reports the current collectibles.

Adds `collectibles_read_race`: 128 readers re-execute in each of 100 rounds and peek the collectibles of a shared root operation, which changes its collectibles in the same round. The readers don't wait for that operation, so the change races with their reads.

### Why?

`read_task_collectibles` read the source's collectibles and made the reader's collectibles dependency current under separate locks. A collectibles change in between still saw the dependency as outdated (not read yet), so `InvalidateDueToCollectiblesChange` made the reader dirty but not stale. The reader's execution then completed with the collectibles it read before the change, and its dirty flag was cleared.

### How?

`read_task_collectibles` locks the source and the reader together with `task_pair`, like output and cell reads already do. A task reading its own collectibles uses the single guard.

### Verification

prs.title: Fix `ImageResponse` prerendering with `--debug-prerender`
prs.author: unstubbable
prs.body:
With Cache Components, `ImageResponse` uses serialized Flight output as the key for image bytes cached during the prospective prerender. Flight debug info can differ between the prospective and final passes, causing cache misses that can make static image routes dynamic under `--debug-prerender`.

The route-handler scheduling changes in #101593 let streaming Flight's immediate work finish within the prerender budget. The React fix react/react#38233 included in #101673 supports lazy decoding after EOF with the debug channel discarded. The image serializer can now use `renderToPipeableStream` and discard debug info through a separate channel, following the pattern in `encryptActionBoundArgs`.

The debug channel still leaves I/O debug chunk references in the main stream. However, React omits this info for work completed before the render's `startTime`. The warm final pass therefore drops records emitted in the prospective pass. A future `startTime` makes both passes omit those records and references.

The abort-signal change proposed in #101509 does not address the key mismatch. In the original reproduction, serialization completes in both passes, but the final cache lookup fails because the emitted debug info differs.

The metadata-image suite now runs with and without `--debug-prerender` and covers deferred trees, image variants, and request-dependent images.

Closes #101509
Fixes #101501

prs.title: Turbopack: release freed memory right after project shutdown
prs.author: sokra
prs.body:
## What?

After `project.shutdown()` resolves in a Turbopack `next build`, return the memory that was freed by dropping the turbo-tasks storage to the OS right away. Until now it stayed resident for another 6–10s.

Part of #100250.

## Why?

`TurboTasksBackend::stop` already drops the task storage (`storage.drop_contents()`). Even so, on a large generated App Router app (5000 routes, 32 CPUs) the main process stayed at **~12.5–13 GB RSS** once shutdown resolved. It only fell to ~1 GB in steps over the next 6–10s, while the static generation workers were already loading their page bundles. That overlap directly raises the peak memory of the build's process tree.

Root cause, found with RSS timelines, mimalloc commit stats and thread counts:

- mimalloc keeps each page in the heap of the thread that allocated it. A free from another thread only queues the block on that page, and the owning thread has to collect its heap before the page becomes free.
- Tokio scheduler workers collect on every park (`on_thread_park` → `TurboMalloc::thread_park`). **Blocking-pool threads have no such hook.**
- Many blocking-pool threads used to be scheduler workers that did compilation and persistence work. They handed their worker role to a new thread in `block_in_place` (used by `scope_bounded`) and own a large share of the heap. During shutdown the process grows from 44 to 75 threads.
- Those threads only collect when they exit after Tokio's 10s idle keep-alive. RSS dropped in step with the thr

prs.title: turbopack: use static for shared rcstr! values and hardcode magic identifiers
prs.author: lukesandberg
prs.body:
### What?

Gives shared `rcstr!` values in Turbopack and the Next.js Rust crates one consistent form:

- **Shared values** (used at 2+ sites) are now `static`, keeping their existing visibility. Before, there were three patterns mixed together: `const`, `static`, and zero-arg `fn foo() -> RcStr { rcstr!(..) }`.
- **Single-use values** are inlined as `rcstr!(..)` where they're used, unless a named `static` reads better. The ones kept as named statics are the babel loader/plugin names, the Google Fonts user agent, and the mangle table's `SINGLE_ITEM_IDENTIFIER`.
- **Required exceptions:** `default_display` in `next_font/local/request.rs` stays a function because `#[serde(default = "...")]` needs one. No `const` turned out to be required. The `const` items in `turbo-rcstr`'s own unit tests stay as they are, because they exist to test const evaluation.
- **Mangled magic identifiers** are now hardcoded instead of computed at runtime by `magic_identifier::mangle`:
  - `MAGIC_IDENTIFIER_DEFAULT_EXPORT` was a `LazyLock<RcStr>` only because `mangle` isn't `const`. It is now a plain `static` built from a precomputed string.
  - The `import.meta` and `__webpack_exports_info__` identifiers were mangled on every call. They are now built from precomputed strings with swc's cached `atom!`.
  - A unit test asserts each hardcoded value equals `mangle(<source>)`, so the constants can't drift from the algorithm.

### Why?

- **Consistency:** one form for shared strings makes them easier to read

prs.title: turbo-tasks-backend: keep the active count inline
prs.author: lukesandberg
prs.body:
## Summary

A task's activeness was an `ActivenessState` lazy field. The field was added when the task became active and removed when it became inactive, and tasks do that a few times per build: about 17.8M activations on a large app with 7.9M tasks. Every one of those added and removed a lazy field. The removals mostly happened long after the task completed, so each also left an empty 40-byte slot in the lazy field vec.

The state is now split:

- **The active count** lives inline in an `i16`. It fits in `TaskStorage`'s padding, so `TaskStorage` stays 128 bytes.
- **The lazy `activeness_state` field** holds the rarely needed rest: root and active-until-clean state, the clean event, and the count while it doesn't fit the `i16`. Only roots, tasks kept active until clean, and very widely shared tasks need it.
- **Activeness is unchanged in meaning:** a task is active while either is present, which covers a negative count during races.

Most activations are now just a counter update. The call sites go through an `ActivenessAccessors` trait (`is_active`, `has_positive_active_count`, `add_active_count`, …).

prs.author: sokra
prs.body:
## Summary

#100288 moved SST block-directory validation into `BlockOffsets`: the whole directory is read with `pread` and validated once when a file is opened, and every block read goes through `BlockOffsets::block_range`. That covers the runtime readers this PR originally hardened. What's left here is the `sst_inspect` tool, which still read SST files with unchecked arithmetic, plus end-to-end tests.

- **`sst_inspect` reuses the runtime validation.** `BlockOffsets` is now public, with `read` and `block_range` (both documented). `sst_inspect` builds its block directory with `BlockOffsets::read` and locates every block through `block_range`. Before this change it panicked on several kinds of corrupt file:

  | Corrupt file | Before |
  | --- | --- |
  | File shorter than its block directory | subtract with overflow |
  | Zero blocks | `block_count - 1` overflow |
  | Out-of-range block offset | slice panic |
  | Out-of-range block index | slice panic |
  | Index block ending inside the directory | reported as a checksum mismatch |

- **Zero-block files.** `BlockOffsets::read` accepts an empty directory, and the runtime rejects it separately when reading the index block. `sst_inspect` now rejects zero blocks explicitly before it looks for the index block.
